passage: The power had gone out in the village again, so the whole lane sat on Dadaji's charpai under the neem tree. Anand, nine, held the lantern. Sunaina, his cousin, kept poking him to stop swinging it. Dadaji told them about the old stepwell behind the temple, how the king's daughter had it dug during a drought so no one had to walk to the river. "She sold her own bangles to pay the workers," he said. Anand frowned. "Then why is it named after the king?" Dadaji laughed. "Good question. Stories remember some people louder than others." The next morning Anand and Sunaina went to the stepwell and counted the steps. Sunaina found a small carved bangle on the third pillar.

qa.q: Where did the family sit when the power went out?
qa.a: They sat on Dadaji's charpai under the neem tree in the lane.

qa.q: Why did Anand frown when he heard the story?
qa.a: He was puzzled and felt it was unfair that the king got the name when his daughter had sold her bangles; he was noticing whose part the story leaves out.

qa.q: How could Dadaji keep Anand's curiosity about local history going?
qa.a: He could take the children to the stepwell or to older neighbours so they can collect more versions of the story and compare them.

qa.q: What is it like for Sunaina to find the carved bangle on the pillar?
qa.a: It probably makes the story feel real to her, as if the daughter's part is written into the stone even if the name is not.

grounding: It shows a child hearing a local legend from a grandparent, questioning its lesson and linking it to a real place in the village.

passage: Every Friday in Mr Okafor's flat in Leeds, Chidi's grandfather told one tale about Tortoise, the clever, greedy trickster from home. Gabriel, Chidi's best mate from the flat upstairs, had started coming down just for this. Tonight Tortoise tricked the birds into lending him feathers, then ate the whole feast himself. The birds took their feathers back, and Tortoise fell and cracked his shell. "That's why his shell has patches," said Grandpa. Gabriel grinned. "My nan tells one where the fox steals the cheese from a crow. Same thing, really. Greedy one loses." Chidi looked pleased and a little proud. "Next Friday you tell yours," he said. "Then Grandpa can check if it's the same lesson."

qa.q: What did Tortoise do with the feast in Grandpa's story?
qa.a: He ate the whole feast himself after borrowing feathers from the birds.

qa.q: What does Chidi's pleased, proud look suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: He seems glad that his friend enjoys his family's stories and sees them as worth comparing, which makes his heritage feel valued.

qa.q: How could Grandpa build on Gabriel's idea of swapping stories?
qa.a: He could let each boy tell a tale and then ask them together what the two stories are trying to teach and how they differ.

qa.q: How might Gabriel see the Friday stories now?
qa.a: He probably sees them as a fun ritual he belongs to, and a way to notice that his nan's stories share lessons with Chidi's family's tales.

grounding: It shows children learning a folk tale and its moral from a grandparent and linking it to a story from another tradition.

passage: The Class 5 trip to the district museum started badly. Rashmi's group got the dusty room with the old coins and a broken plough. "This is boring," Bhavna whispered. Then the guide, a retired schoolteacher, picked up a clay lamp. "Two hundred years ago, the people of your town lit this during the salt march meeting in the market square," she said. "Your market. The one near the sweet shop." Rashmi's eyes widened. She had bought jalebi there on Sunday. Bhavna leaned in. By the end, the two girls had filled a whole page of notes and argued about which street the crowd had walked down. On the bus home, Rashmi pressed her face to the window as they passed the square.

qa.q: What object did the guide pick up in the museum room?
qa.a: She picked up a clay lamp.

qa.q: Why did Rashmi's eyes widen when the guide mentioned the market?
qa.a: She suddenly realised the history happened in a place she knows, near the sweet shop where she bought jalebi on Sunday, so it felt personal and exciting.

qa.q: What could a teacher learn from how the guide changed the girls' mood?
qa.a: Linking old objects to places children already know turns dull facts into their own story, so starting from the town's streets could help other lessons too.

qa.q: What would change if the guide had only read out dates from a label?
qa.a: Bhavna might have stayed bored, and the girls would not have argued over the route or looked at the square differently on the way home.

grounding: It shows children in a school museum visit connecting their region's history to familiar streets.

passage: I'm Maria. I've lived across from Simran's family in this old part of Ahmedabad for twenty years. This winter I kept seeing her, nine or ten years old, sitting on the steps of the stepwell near our lane with a notebook. Every evening she'd stop the elderly men playing cards and ask them things. Once I heard her say, 'But who built it? Was it a queen?' One uncle told her a long story about a queen who built it so travellers would never go thirsty. Simran wrote fast, tongue poking out. Later she knocked on my door to ask what I remembered of the well when it still had water. I don't know what drew her there. But she looked happy doing it.

qa.q: Where did Maria keep seeing Simran sit in the evenings?
qa.a: On the steps of the stepwell near their lane, with a notebook.

qa.q: What does Simran writing fast with her tongue poking out suggest about her?
qa.a: It suggests she was absorbed and curious about the story, though Maria can't be sure what drew her.

qa.q: How could Simran's teacher support her interest in local history?
qa.a: The teacher could invite her to share the stories with the class and help her compare them with a library book about the city.

qa.q: How might the elderly card players feel about Simran's questions?
qa.a: They might enjoy being asked, glad that a child cares about the old stories they carry.

grounding: An observer sees a child gathering local history and a legend about her area from elders.

passage: Monday: In the Hindi period, Avni, ten, yawned through the Ramayana chapter. 'Old stories,' she whispered to Kashish. 'Nothing to do with us.' Thursday: At Kashish's house, her grandmother told them about the little squirrel who rolled in sand and shook it onto the stones while the monkeys built the great bridge. 'Such a tiny thing,' said Nani, 'and Ram stroked her back with thanks.' Avni sat very still. 'So even small help counts?' she asked. Next Monday: When class was cleaning the garden, Avni saw the youngest girl carrying just one pot. Kashish laughed. Avni said, 'Squirrel help. It counts.' The girl beamed. Avni asked the teacher for the next chapter.

qa.q: What did the squirrel do while the bridge was being built?
qa.a: She rolled in sand and shook it onto the stones.

qa.q: What was Avni thinking when she 'sat very still' listening to Nani?
qa.a: She was realising the old story had a meaning for her own life, that even small help matters.

qa.q: How did Avni use the story's moral in real life?
qa.a: She defended the youngest girl carrying one pot, saying small help counts, instead of laughing.

qa.q: How might the youngest girl have felt when Avni spoke up?
qa.a: She likely felt valued and proud that her small effort was noticed. 😊

grounding: Shows a child coming to see the moral of an epic story and applying it.

passage:
Aadhya, you walk past that old stepwell every day and never look at it. Sit, and let your Amandeep Nanaji tell you its story.
Long ago, before my grandfather was born, there was a drought in our village near Patan. No rain for three years. The rich families had their own wells. The poor had nothing.
A widow called Roopba sold her gold bangles and hired diggers to make a well for everyone, with steps so even children could reach the water. People laughed at her. Then the water came, cold and deep, and nobody laughed again.
That is why, at every wedding in our village, the bride pours the first water from that stepwell. We remember that one person can care for everyone.

qa.q: What did Roopba sell to hire diggers?
qa.a: She sold her gold bangles.

qa.q: How did Roopba probably feel when people laughed at her?
qa.a: She probably felt hurt but determined, believing the well would help everyone.

qa.q: What choice in the story made the biggest difference, and why?
qa.a: Roopba's choice to spend her bangles on a well for everyone, because it saved the whole village in the drought.

qa.q: How might the poor families have felt when the water came?
qa.a: They would have felt deeply relieved and grateful, knowing someone had cared for them.

grounding: A grandfather tells his granddaughter a local history of the village stepwell and its moral of care.

passage:
The heritage walk through the old city of Hyderabad was supposed to take two hours. Then the rain came down hard, and the class had to squeeze under the arch of an old gate.
Noor, eleven, was annoyed. She'd wanted to see the palace.
Their guide, Madhuri, didn't waste the time. She pointed at the carvings above them. “This gate was built after a great flood. The people rebuilt their city together, rich and poor, carrying stones. Look, the carvings show their hands.”
Noor looked up. There were hands, dozens of them, carved in stone.
By the time the rain stopped, Noor had drawn every hand in her notebook.

qa.q: What did the carvings above the gate show?
qa.a: They showed the hands of the people who rebuilt the city.

qa.q: How did Noor feel about the heritage walk as the rain stopped it, and later?
qa.a: She felt annoyed at first, then curious and absorbed once she saw the carvings.

qa.q: What did Madhuri do that turned the rain into a good lesson?
qa.a: She used the time under the gate to tell its story and point out the carvings.

qa.q: How might the other students feel about the gate after the story?
qa.a: They may feel more connected to their city's history and see the gate differently.

grounding: Sheltering from rain, an eleven-year-old learns local history and its message of rebuilding together.

passage:
At bedtime in their Pune flat, Chandrika told Aadhya, nine, the story of the monkey and the crocodile. The crocodile's wife wanted the monkey's heart. The monkey was clever and said he'd left his heart in the tree, and escaped.
The next evening, Aadhya's little brother Neel was crying because a boy at the park had tricked him out of his ball.
Aadhya sat beside him. “Listen. Once there was a monkey…” She told the whole story, adding sound effects.
“So what does it mean?” Neel sniffed.
Aadhya thought. “Keep your head when someone tricks you. And don't trust everyone just because they're nice.”
Chandrika, listening at the door, smiled.

qa.q: Where did the monkey say he'd left his heart?
qa.a: He said he'd left his heart in the tree.

qa.q: How did Chandrika feel listening at the door?
qa.a: She felt proud and happy, seeing Aadhya pass the story on.

qa.q: How did Aadhya use the folk tale to help Neel?
qa.a: She told the story and explained its lesson about keeping your head and being careful whom you trust.

qa.q: How might Neel feel after hearing the story?
qa.a: He probably feels comforted and a bit wiser about being tricked.

grounding: A nine-year-old retells a folk tale and its moral to comfort her little brother.

passage:
"Sarita Bua, why is the old fort wall broken on one side?" Ritu asked as they walked past it to the market.
"Ah. There's a story. Three hundred years ago, the queen here refused to hand over the town to an invading army."
"Did she fight?"
"She did. The wall broke where the cannons hit. But she held the fort for forty days."
"Forty days! Then what?"
"They made peace. She kept the town, but paid a tax."
Ritu looked at the wall again. "So she didn't win or lose?"
"She protected her people. That's what the town remembers."
Ritu touched the broken stones. "I'm going to write about her for my project."

qa.q: How many days did the queen hold the fort?
qa.a: Forty days.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling when she touched the broken stones?
qa.a: Ritu felt moved and proud, connecting the wall to the queen's story.

qa.q: How could Sarita Bua help Ritu learn more for her project?
qa.a: She could take Ritu to a local library or museum, or to an elder who knows more about the town's past.

qa.q: How does Sarita Bua see the queen's story?
qa.a: Sarita Bua sees it as a story about protecting people, not about winning or losing.

grounding: A child learns a piece of her town's history from her aunt.

passage:
When I was in Class 5, I thought history was just dates. Then my friend Akash's grandfather took us to the old church near our village in Goa.
He showed us a stone with carved ships. "This is where the fishermen prayed before the big storm of 1890," he said. "They all went out together, and they all came back, because they tied their boats to each other."
Akash and I stared at the ships. That night I kept thinking about the tied boats.
Our teacher later read us a Panchatantra story about doves caught in a net who flew away together. The same idea.
I'm Francis. I still think of that stone when I work in a group.

qa.q: What was carved on the stone?
qa.a: Ships.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling that night, thinking about the tied boats?
qa.a: Francis felt fascinated and moved by how the fishermen survived together.

qa.q: What could Francis do to learn more local stories?
qa.a: Francis could ask other elders in the village about old events and visit other places like the church.

qa.q: How might Akash's grandfather feel sharing this story?
qa.a: He likely feels proud and happy to pass the village's history to the children.

grounding: A young person recalls learning a local story whose moral matched a folk tale.

passage:
Class 5 teacher's note.
This week we read the story of Ekalavya from the Mahabharata. Most students liked the archery. Uma was quiet.
Today she asked, "Was Drona fair to take his thumb?" The class split. Some said Ekalavya should obey the teacher. Others said Drona was unfair.
Uma said, "The story is great, but I think the lesson is that talent should not depend on who you are."
I asked them to write what the story teaches and whether they agree. Uma wrote two pages.
Next week, Anand's grandfather will visit to tell a folk tale from our district. — Mrs Joshi

qa.q: Which story did the class read this week?
qa.a: The story of Ekalavya from the Mahabharata.

qa.q: What might Uma have been feeling when she was quiet?
qa.a: Uma may have felt troubled and uneasy about the unfairness in the story.

qa.q: What did Mrs Joshi do that helped the class think about the story's moral?
qa.a: She let them discuss both sides and asked them to write what the story teaches and whether they agree.

qa.q: How might classmates who said Ekalavya should obey see Uma's view?
qa.a: They might find it new and start to see the story from a fairness angle too.

grounding: A teacher notes a child thinking critically about the moral of an epic.

passage:
Lokesh's diary, Saturday
Our town's stepwell is just a dry, smelly pit now. I always thought it was boring. Today Anand Uncle, who runs the reading room near the bus stand, took four of us there and told us how it was built.
Long ago there was a drought for three years. The rich family wanted to dig a well only for their own fields. An old woman who sold curd said, "Water that belongs to one house dries up in one house." So the whole town dug together, even kids carried baskets of mud.
Anand Uncle said that's why the steps go down on all four sides: so nobody has to wait for anyone else.
I looked at the steps differently after that. I'm going to draw them tomorrow.

qa.q: Why do the stepwell's steps go down on all four sides, according to Anand Uncle?
qa.a: So nobody has to wait for anyone else.

qa.q: How did Lokesh's feelings about the stepwell change?
qa.a: Lokesh first found the stepwell boring, but after the story felt curious and interested enough to want to draw the steps.

qa.q: How could a teacher use a local story like this in class?
qa.a: A teacher could take students to the place, tell its story, and ask what the town's choice teaches about sharing today.

qa.q: How might Anand Uncle feel when the children look at the steps differently?
qa.a: Anand Uncle might feel pleased and hopeful that the town's history, and its lesson about sharing, will be remembered.

grounding: Shows a child learning a piece of local history and its moral about sharing from a community elder.

passage:
On the last night of the Dussehra Ramlila, Tejas sat on the school ground in his village, bored. He had seen Ravana burn every year.
"Why does Nani care so much?" he muttered.
Simran, his cousin, pulled him to where Nani sat on a mat. Nani pointed at the stage made of bullock carts. "Seventy years ago the river flooded the temple yard. Everyone said, no Ramlila this year. My father said the story is for hard years most of all. So they joined carts and did it here."
Tejas watched the actor playing Hanuman leap across the carts. "So that's why it's on carts?"
"That's why," said Simran. "We're sitting in the flood story too."
When the effigy caught fire, Tejas clapped louder than usual.

qa.q: What was the Ramlila stage made of?
qa.a: The stage was made of bullock carts.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling at the start of the evening, and what shows it?
qa.a: Tejas felt bored, because he sat muttering that he had seen Ravana burn every year.

qa.q: What small step helped Tejas care about the Ramlila?
qa.a: Simran taking him to Nani to hear the flood story connected the old epic to his own village's history.

qa.q: How does Nani see the Ramlila differently from Tejas at first?
qa.a: For Nani it holds her family's memory of getting through a hard year, not just a show she has seen before.

grounding: Illustrates a child connecting an epic performance to the local history and meaning his family attaches to it.

passage:
The lanterns were already swinging along the Hanoi street when Liam arrived for his first Mid-Autumn Festival. Tuan handed him a paper star lantern and pointed at the full moon.
"See the dark patch? That's Cuoi, sitting under a banyan tree."
"Why is he stuck up there?"
Tuan told it the way his grandmother did. Cuoi's magic banyan tree could heal people, but it had one rule: never water it with dirty water. Cuoi forgot, the tree flew up to the sky, and he grabbed its roots and went with it.
"So the moral is… keep promises?" Liam asked.
"Grandma says it's that small carelessness can cost big things."
Liam looked up again. The dark patch did look like someone sitting, waiting.

qa.q: What rule came with Cuoi's magic banyan tree?
qa.a: Never water it with dirty water.

qa.q: What does Liam's question about the moral suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: Liam seemed curious and interested, trying to understand the meaning of the story, not just the plot.

qa.q: How could Tuan make the story even more meaningful for Liam?
qa.a: Tuan could ask Liam if there is a moon story in his own family, so they can compare what each teaches.

qa.q: What is it like for Tuan to tell the story the way his grandmother does?
qa.a: Tuan probably feels proud and close to his grandmother, passing on her words to a new friend.

grounding: Shows a child sharing a festival folk tale and its moral with a visiting friend.

passage:
On the first day of the summer camp at the Kannur community library, Elizabeth Miss unrolled an old map of the town. "See this fort by the sea? Four hundred years old. Traders from far away came here for pepper."
Vaibhav, ten, yawned. "History is just dates."
"Then let's not do dates." She handed out paper crowns and cardboard swords. "Today you are the fort guards. Tomorrow, the traders."
By noon Vaibhav was shouting orders from the library steps, pretending to spot ships. He asked, "Did the guards ever win?"
"Sometimes. Sometimes they made deals. Come to the fort on Saturday and find out."
On Saturday, Vaibhav was the first one at the gate, notebook in hand.

qa.q: What did traders come to the town for?
qa.a: Traders from far away came here for pepper.

qa.q: How can you tell Vaibhav's feeling about history changed?
qa.a: He went from yawning to eagerly shouting orders and being first at the fort gate, which shows he became curious and excited.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth Miss do that made history come alive?
qa.a: She turned the local story into a role-play and invited the children to visit the real fort, instead of teaching dates.

qa.q: What would change if Elizabeth Miss had only read out dates?
qa.a: Vaibhav might have stayed bored and never cared about his town's past or wanted to visit the fort.

grounding: Shows a child connecting with the history of his own region through play and a visit to a local fort.
